reveal.question: Which is the odd one out?
reveal.answer: Uranium. Coal, oil and gas are fossil fuels we burn. Uranium is a nuclear fuel: nothing is burned, so no carbon dioxide.

learn.heading: Non-renewable energy resources

items: A non-renewable resource is used up faster than it can be replaced.
Once it is used, it is gone. One day it will run out.
Fossil fuels: coal, oil and natural gas. Formed from dead plants and animals over millions of years.
Nuclear fuel: uranium. It is not a fossil fuel and it is not burned.

learn.imageDescription: graph of known oil, gas and coal reserves running out between 2011 and 2081

learn.heading: Uses, and why we rely on them

items: Transport: petrol, diesel and kerosene (jet fuel), all made from oil.
Electricity: coal, gas and nuclear power stations.
Heating: natural gas boilers, oil and coal.
Concentrated store of energy: a little fuel releases a lot of energy.
Reliable: available day and night, whatever the weather.
Easy to store and transport.

learn.imageDescription: blue natural gas flame on a cooker hob

learn.heading: Problems with burning fossil fuels

items: Carbon dioxide (CO_2): a greenhouse gas. Adds to global warming and climate change.
Sulfur dioxide (SO_2): dissolves in rain water to make acid rain.
Nitrogen dioxide (NO_2): causes acid rain and breathing problems.
Damages trees, kills fish in lakes and wears away stone buildings.

learn.imageDescription: cartoon storm cloud with acid rain falling

learn.heading: Fossil fuels or nuclear?

rows.b: Uranium nuclei split (fission). Nothing is burned.
No CO_2 or SO_2 while running
Extremely concentrated: one fuel pellet = 1 tonne of coal

rows.a: Reliable. Gas starts in minutes, coal in hours
rows.b: Reliable, but takes days to start up
Radioactive waste stays dangerous for thousands of years
Expensive to build and close down. Small risk of accidents

build.q: Why is natural gas used to heat most homes in the UK?
options: It is a concentrated, reliable store of energy
build.explanation: A little gas releases a lot of energy, and it is available whenever it is needed.

build.q: Which fuel is made from oil and used in cars?
build.explanation: Petrol and diesel are both made from crude oil.

questions.q: Describe how the amount of carbon dioxide changes after 1800.
questions.a: It stays near 285 ppm until about 1850, then rises faster and faster, to about 410 ppm by 2020.

questions.q: How much has the average global temperature risen since 1850?
Suggest why carbon dioxide rose after 1850.
questions.a: People began burning large amounts of fossil fuels in factories, power stations and vehicles.

build.q: Which gas from burning fossil fuels causes acid rain?
build.explanation: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water and makes it acidic.

build.q: Why does a nuclear power station not release carbon dioxide while it runs?
build.explanation: Energy comes from splitting uranium nuclei (fission), not from burning.

build.q: Which is a disadvantage of nuclear power?
build.explanation: Nuclear waste stays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored safely.

mastering.q: Coal releases 900 g of CO_2 per kWh. Gas releases 400 g per kWh. A town uses 2000 kWh each hour. How much CO_2 does gas save per hour?
A town's coal power station is closing. Evaluate replacing it with a gas or a nuclear power station. Give a reasoned choice.
mastering.a: Gas: cheaper, starts quickly, but still releases CO_2 and will run out. Nuclear: no CO_2, very concentrated fuel, but radioactive waste, expensive, slow to start. A choice backed by a reason.
indicativeContent: Gas releases less CO_2 than coal, but still adds to global warming
Gas power stations are cheaper to build than nuclear
Gas stations start in minutes, so they can follow changes in demand
Nuclear releases no CO_2 or SO_2 while running
Nuclear produces radioactive waste that stays dangerous for thousands of years
Nuclear is expensive to build and to close down, and takes days to start
Both fuels are non-renewable and will run out
A clear final choice, supported by at least one reason
